# Arroz Caldo 🇵🇭

::: {.dish-meta}
**Region:** Philippines  ·  **Family:** Porridge / congee
**Serves:** 4–6  ·  **Active time:** 30 minutes  ·  **Total:** 1 hour
:::

When a Filipino is sick, cold, or simply in need of comfort, this is the bowl
that appears. *Arroz caldo* — "rice broth" — is a ginger-forward chicken congee,
the local expression of a dish that travels the whole rice-eating world under a
dozen names.

## The story

Arroz caldo sits at a crossroads of influences. Its base is Chinese *congee*,
brought by traders and immigrants centuries ago; its Spanish name is a legacy of
three hundred years of colonial rule (Spanish colonizers called nearly every
rice porridge *arroz caldo*). Filipino cooks made it their own with a heavy hand
of ginger, a hit of fish sauce, and a squeeze of *calamansi*.

Unlike a plain Cantonese congee, arroz caldo is unapologetically savory and
aromatic — as much a chicken dish as a rice one.

## Ingredients

**The porridge**

- 1 kg (2.2 lb) bone-in chicken thighs and drumsticks
- 200 g (1 cup) glutinous rice (*malagkit*), or 1:1 glutinous and jasmine
- 1 large onion, diced
- 8 cloves garlic, minced
- 1 large thumb (50 g) ginger, julienned — be generous
- 3 tbsp fish sauce (*patis*), plus more to taste
- 1.8–2 L (8 cups) chicken stock or water, plus more as needed
- 2 tbsp neutral oil
- Pinch of ground turmeric or a little saffron (optional, for golden color)
- Black pepper

**To serve**

- Toasted garlic (fry the extra minced garlic in oil until golden — don't skip)
- Sliced scallions, calamansi or lime wedges
- Jammy or hard-boiled eggs, halved
- Fish sauce and chili oil at the table

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
**Gluten-free · dairy-free:** naturally both — rice, ginger, chicken, and fish
sauce. Just pick a **gluten-free fish sauce and chili oil** (most are, but a few
add wheat), and if you swap in bouillon anywhere, make it a certified GF one.
:::

## Method

1. Season the chicken with pepper. In a heavy pot, heat the oil and brown the
   chicken pieces on all sides; remove and set aside. They needn't cook
   through — you want the fond.
2. In the same pot, soften the onion 3–4 minutes. Add the ginger and garlic and
   fry until deeply fragrant, 2 minutes. Stir in the turmeric.
3. Return the chicken. Add the rinsed glutinous rice and toast, stirring, 1
   minute so each grain is coated in the aromatic fat.
4. Pour in the fish sauce and the stock. Bring to a boil, then drop to a
   simmer.
5. Cook uncovered, **stirring often** to stop the rice catching, 40–45 minutes.
   The rice will break down and the porridge will thicken to a loose,
   spoon-coating consistency. Add hot stock whenever it gets too thick — arroz
   caldo should flow, not stand.
6. Lift out the chicken, shred or leave on the bone as you like, and return it.
   Taste and correct with fish sauce and pepper. It should be assertively
   savory.
7. Ladle into bowls and pile on the garnishes: toasted garlic first (always),
   then scallion, egg, and a wedge of calamansi to squeeze over.

## The two non-negotiables

- **Ginger, in quantity.** It's the soul of the dish; a timid amount makes a
  bland one.
- **Toasted garlic on top.** The crunchy, nutty *toasted* garlic (distinct from
  the garlic cooked into the base) is what makes people close their eyes on the
  first spoonful.

## Make it yours

- **Goto** is the offal version, made with tripe — a beloved street-food variant.
- Vegetarian? Skip the chicken, build the base on mushrooms, and use a robust
  vegetable stock; the ginger and toasted garlic still carry it.
- For extra richness, some cooks stir in a little of the rendered chicken skin,
  crisped separately, at the end.

::: {.callout-tip}
## It thickens as it sits
Congee-family dishes keep drinking liquid. Cook it a touch looser than you want
to serve it, and keep a kettle of hot stock nearby to loosen leftovers.
:::
